title: Python's urlparse doesn't raise on garbage - "not a url" parses "successfully" into an empty scheme and host
assumption: If a string isn't a valid URL, the URL-parsing function you call will raise an error, so "it didn't throw" is good evidence the input was a real URL.

input.description: User-submitted text in a field that is supposed to be a URL (a profile link, a webhook target, a redirect destination), validated with `urlparse` and a check like `if result.netloc: ...` or simply `try: urlparse(x) except: reject`.

what_goes_wrong: `urlparse("not a url")` does not raise - it returns a `ParseResult` with empty `scheme` and `netloc` and the whole input shoved into `.path`. JavaScript's `new URL("not a url")` does the opposite: it throws `TypeError: Invalid URL` immediately, because the WHATWG algorithm requires an absolute URL (or a base to resolve against) and fails loudly otherwise.
why: Python's `urllib.parse.urlparse` implements RFC 3986's generic syntax as a permissive, almost mechanical split on delimiter characters (`://`, `@`, `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`) - if the expected delimiters for scheme/netloc aren't present, it doesn't fail, it just leaves those fields empty and puts everything into whichever component comes last in the fallback order (`path`). It was designed to parse URI *references* (which may be relative, schemeless fragments) permissively, not to validate that a string is a complete, dereferenceable URL. The WHATWG `URL` constructor is deliberately the opposite: it exists specifically to parse (and validate) a resolvable URL, so it throws on anything that doesn't resolve to one. (It is not literally exception-free: an unbalanced IPv6 bracket such as `http://[::1` raises ValueError, and reading `.port` raises for an out-of-range port - but ordinary non-URL text goes straight through.)

repros.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
r = urlparse("not a url")
print(r)
print(bool(r.scheme), bool(r.netloc))
repros.expected_output:
ParseResult(scheme='', netloc='', path='not a url', params='', query='', fragment='')
False False

fix: Never treat "urlparse didn't raise" as proof of a valid URL in Python. Explicitly check that both `scheme` is one of the schemes you accept (e.g. `http`/`https`) and `netloc` is non-empty, or use a stricter validator before trusting the result.

sources.title: WHATWG URL Standard: URL parsing failures

test_cases.note: their_is_valid_url(text) must explicitly reject this - checking only whether urlparse() raised is not enough, since urlparse never raises on this input.
